inputs.need:
I am a nurse practitioner with the palliative care consult team at a 600-bed teaching hospital. Our medical and oncology wards are supposed to document advance care planning conversations in a structured note, but when we looked at 120 patients who died in hospital last year, only 22 had any documented conversation about their goals before the last week of life, and most of those were a single line such as 'discussed, not for resuscitation'. The hospital wants a better approach: a serious illness conversation template in the electronic health record, a prompt when a patient meets triggers (for example a second unplanned admission within six months, or a clinician answering no to the question whether they would be surprised if the patient died within a year), and a short communication skills session for ward doctors and nurses.

I am not sure how to evaluate this. We could run a stepped-wedge randomised trial across the six medical and oncology wards, which the hospital research office likes. Or we could start with a retrospective chart review of what gets documented now and compare it with what is documented after the template goes live. I have read papers saying that structured prompts double documentation and others saying the notes turn into tick boxes that do not reflect what patients want, so I am not even sure documentation is the right thing to measure.

I need help deciding what to do first and what to measure: how often conversations are documented, the quality of what is written, whether care matches what patients said they wanted, and what families experience. We have a small internal grant, a data analyst for a few hours a month, and ward managers who are supportive but worried about workload.
inputs.constraints: Internal grant of 15,000 for one year. Data analyst available 6 hours per month. Ward staff can attend at most one 60-minute training session each. The template can only go live in the record build team's February 2027 release.

response.title: Serious illness conversation template and prompts on medical and oncology wards: what to test first
response.subtitle: Evaluation design not yet settled
response.statement: Only 22 of 120 patients who died in the hospital last year had a documented goals-of-care conversation before the last week of life, and most notes recorded only resuscitation status. The hospital plans a serious illness conversation template with prognostic prompts and a short skills session on six medical and oncology wards from February 2027. response.currentPractice: A free-text advance care planning note, completed inconsistently; conversations mostly happen late or not at all.
response.whyNow: The template is scheduled for the February 2027 release, a small internal grant is available, and the research office wants an evaluation plan.

records.title: Serious illness conversation prompts and documented goals-of-care discussions on medical wards: a cluster randomised trial
records.authors: Oyelowo-Bergman A, Castillo-Faraday N, Iwu-Hendricks M
records.abstract: We randomly allocated 12 medical wards to electronic prompts for serious illness conversations with a 90-minute clinician training session, or to usual care. Among 1,480 patients who met prognostic triggers, documented goals-of-care discussions before the last week of life rose from 18 to 41 percent on intervention wards and were unchanged on control wards. Documentation happened a median of 19 days earlier. The trial did not assess the content of the notes and did not measure whether care matched patients' stated goals. Staff on intervention wards reported that the prompts added about four minutes per eligible patient.

records.title: Tick-box documentation after an electronic advance care planning template: a content analysis of hospital notes
records.abstract: We analysed 400 advance care planning notes written in the year before and the year after a hospital introduced a structured electronic template. The number of notes rose sharply after the template, but 63 percent of notes contained only resuscitation status and 12 percent documented anything about the patient's values or priorities. On a six-point quality score, the mean was 2.1 before and 2.3 after the template. Notes written by palliative care clinicians scored higher than those written by ward teams. The authors conclude that templates can increase the number of notes without improving what they say.

records.title: A structured template with ward training and the quality of documented advance care planning conversations: a before-after study
records.authors: Achterberg-Nkosi J, Rowan-Takeda L, Faris-Olsen D
records.abstract: On four medical wards we introduced a structured conversation template together with a 60-minute communication skills session and monthly feedback on note quality. Documentation of advance care planning conversations for patients meeting prognostic triggers rose from 21 to 47 percent over nine months. Two trained raters scored a random sample of notes on a six-point quality scale; the mean quality score rose from 1.8 to 3.9 of 6, with the largest gains in documenting patient values and what matters most. The study had no concurrent comparison, and raters knew the period of each note.

records.title: Interventions to improve advance care planning documentation in hospital: a systematic review
records.authors: Mbeki-Sorensen K, Haddad-Pryce E, Olawale-Lund F
records.abstract: We searched five databases for studies of interventions to increase documented advance care planning among hospital inpatients and included 23 studies. Documentation improved in 17 studies, most often after electronic prompts or templates combined with education. Only 5 studies assessed the quality of documentation and only 3 measured whether care received matched patients' documented preferences, with inconsistent results. Most studies were uncontrolled before-after comparisons at single sites. The review recommends that future evaluations measure the content of conversations and patient-centred outcomes, not documentation alone.

records.title: Regional review of advance care planning documentation in acute hospitals
records.authors: Regional End of Life Care Network
records.abstract: This network report reviewed the notes of patients who died in 14 acute hospitals in the region. The median proportion with a documented advance care planning conversation before the last week of life was 19 percent, ranging from 8 to 37 percent between hospitals. Five hospitals used a structured template; their median was 24 percent. Data were collected by local staff with different definitions, and the report does not state the period covered or its year of publication. It recommends a common definition and a quality measure for documented conversations.

records.title: Inter-rater reliability of a six-point quality score for documented serious illness conversations
records.abstract: Two palliative care nurses independently rated 150 documented serious illness conversations on a six-point quality score covering prognosis, values, fears, trade-offs, family involvement and recommendations. Before training, agreement was moderate (kappa 0.48). After a two-hour calibration session with worked examples, agreement rose to kappa 0.71. Rating took a median of 6 minutes per note. Notes that recorded only resuscitation status were rated consistently low. The authors recommend calibration and double rating of a sample when the score is used to evaluate an intervention.

records.title: Bereaved family members' views of end-of-life care planning in hospital: a postal questionnaire study
records.abstract: We sent a postal questionnaire to the next of kin of 600 patients who died in two hospitals, three to six months after the death. The response rate was 34 percent, lower among families of younger patients and in deprived neighbourhoods. Families who recalled a conversation about goals of care more often reported that care matched the patient's wishes (72 percent compared with 51 percent). Families valued being included in conversations and wanted clearer explanations of what treatments would and would not do. Non-response limits how far the results apply to all bereaved families.

response.synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level; one has no stated year. A cluster randomised trial and most studies in a systematic review show that prompts and templates increase documented conversations. The records conflict on quality: a before-after study with training and feedback reported large gains in note quality, while a content analysis after a template alone found notes that mostly recorded resuscitation status and quality scores that barely moved. Only a few studies measured whether care matched patients' goals. A six-point quality score can be rated reliably after calibration, and a family questionnaire reached about a third of bereaved relatives. Documentation is achievable; whether it reflects real conversations is uncertain.
response.gradeRationale: One randomised trial for documentation, but conflicting uncontrolled evidence on quality, few patient-centred outcomes, and one undated grey report; certainty that the template improves conversations, not only notes, is low.
response.summary: Seven retrieved records appraised; five claims, one with high uncertainty because the evidence conflicts; overall certainty low.

response.reading: Prompts and templates reliably increase the number of notes, but the conflict between the before-after and content-analysis studies shows that the number of notes and the quality of conversations can come apart. Training and feedback may be what separates the two. A trial would depend on outcomes the hospital has never measured: a quality score, goal-concordant care and family reports. Before a stepped-wedge trial, the hospital needs to know whether these can be measured and whether the intervention can be delivered.

response.rationale: Neither a stepped-wedge trial nor a before-after chart review is the right first step. Prompts increase documentation (c1), but whether the notes reflect real conversations is contested (c3), templates alone can produce tick-box notes (c2), and the outcomes a trial would rely on have not been tested here: quality rating needs calibration (c4) and family response is low (c5). A six-month feasibility study on two wards tests delivery, measurement and recruitment against pre-specified progression criteria before six wards are committed to a trial.
alternatives: Stepped-wedge randomised trial across six wards now (deferred: outcomes untested and the evidence on quality conflicts)
Before-after chart review of documentation rates (refused: would count tick-box notes as success)
Implement the template without evaluation (refused: the hospital cannot tell whether conversations improve)
guidelines: CONSORT extension for pilot and feasibility studies (adapted for a non-randomised feasibility study)
response.whyNotMoreComplex: A trial now would spend the hospital's one release window and the grant on outcomes that may not be measurable; the feasibility study answers that at a fraction of the cost.

decision.statement: Before any stepped-wedge trial, run a six-month feasibility study on two wards that tests delivery of the template, prompts and skills session, the reliability of a calibrated quality score and the response of bereaved families, with progression criteria set in advance.

response.overview: Six-month non-randomised feasibility study on two medical and oncology wards, testing delivery of a serious illness conversation template with prompts, a 60-minute skills session and monthly feedback, and the measures a later stepped-wedge trial would use.

response.title: A serious illness conversation template with prompts and skills training on two hospital wards: a feasibility study
response.abstract: Objective: to test whether a serious illness conversation template with prompts, a skills session and feedback can be delivered on two wards, and whether note quality and family-reported outcomes can be measured, before a stepped-wedge trial. Design: six-month non-randomised feasibility study with progression criteria. Results will follow data collection.
response.introduction: Prompts increase documented conversations, but evidence conflicts on whether notes improve in quality, and few studies measure what patients and families experience.
response.methods: Triggered patients on two wards; template, prompts, skills session and feedback; delivery, rater agreement, family response, documentation and quality measured against progression criteria.
response.results: No data have been collected yet. The report will present delivery, kappa, family response and descriptive change against the progression criteria.
response.discussion: The discussion will judge the progression criteria and state whether and how a stepped-wedge trial should proceed.
response.limitations: Two wards, no comparison group, small family sample.
response.conclusion: To be written after analysis; it will not claim an effect of the template.
response.reportingChecklist: CONSORT extension for pilot and feasibility studies, adapted for a non-randomised design
response.summary: Feasibility report structure with results left empty.
